Flame
flām
n. (burning gas; the visible body of fire; rendering Hebrew lahab and shalhebeth, Greek phlox)
From the Latin flamma, from flagro, to burn. Hebrew lahab is a flame and also the blade of a sword — the flashing edge and the flashing fire share a word — which stands behind the flaming sword at the gate of Eden.

Biblical Definition

Flame is the visible body of fire, and in Scripture it is bound to God's presence, God's servants, and God's judgment. The commission of Moses begins in one: “the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush; and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2) — a fire that burns without destroying, which is a fair picture of the God who dwells with sinners without consuming them. Of the angels it is said that God “maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Hebrews 1:7), the verse Paul's argument uses to prove that angels are servants while the Son is addressed as God. Of the second advent it is the mode of judgment: the Lord Jesus shall be revealed “in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thessalonians 1:8). And the Song gives the word its most surprising application, to covenant love: “love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame” (Song of Solomon 8:6) — a love that burns like the fire of God himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

The visible body of fire. It marks God's presence in the bush that burned unconsumed, describes the angels as ministers, attends the second advent in judgment, and figures covenant love as a most vehement flame.

expand to see more

FLAME, n. [L. flamma, from flagro, to burn.] A blaze; burning vapor; vapor in combustion, emitting light and heat.

2. Fire in general; heat; as, the flame of a furnace.

3. Ardor of temper or imagination; warmth of affection; as, the flame of love.

4. In Scripture, of the divine appearing; as, a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush, Exod. 3.

5. Of judgment at the second advent; as, in flaming fire taking vengeance, 2 Thess. 1.

Key Scripture

Exodus 3:2 — "And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed."

Hebrews 1:7 — "And of the angels he saith, Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire."

2 Thessalonians 1:8 — "In flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ:"

Song of Solomon 8:6 — "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame."

Modern Corruption

The wrath of God is now widely treated as an Old Testament residue unworthy of a God of love. 2 Thessalonians 1:8 places flaming vengeance at the return of Christ, and the love of the Song burns with the same fire.

expand to see more

The proposal to keep divine love and discard divine wrath fails on its own terms, because a love indifferent to the destruction of the beloved is not love. Scripture never sets the two in competition; the Song of Solomon 8:6 says the flame of covenant love is a most vehement one — older translators heard in the Hebrew a flame of the LORD himself — and the same fire that warms is the fire that burns what would destroy. Wrath is love's response to evil, and a God incapable of it would be a God indifferent to murder.

The principle to recover is the character of the fire that appeared to Moses. It burned and the bush was not consumed, and this is the mystery the whole Bible works out: how the holy God can dwell in the midst of a sinful people without destroying them. The answer is the cross, where the fire fell on a substitute. Hebrews 1:7 marks the distance between servant and Son by way of the same imagery — the angels are made a flame of fire, but of the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lahab is a flame and also a sword-blade; shalhebeth is a fierce flame, the word in the Song. Greek phlox is a flame, and pur is fire itself.

expand to see more

Hebrew lahab (H3851) — a flame, and also the blade of a sword; hence the flaming sword of Eden.

Hebrew shalhebeth (H7957) — a fierce flame; a most vehement flame in Song of Solomon 8:6.

Hebrew esh (H784) — fire; our God is a consuming fire, Deuteronomy 4:24.

Greek phlox (G5395) — a flame; the flame of fire in which Christ is revealed.

Greek pur (G4442) — fire; the baptism with the Holy Ghost and with fire, Matthew 3:11.

Usage

"Of the divine appearing to Moses: a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush (Exodus 3:2)."

"Of the angels as servants: his ministers a flame of fire (Hebrews 1:7)."

"Of the second advent: in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God (2 Thessalonians 1:8)."
